title: Innovation and Emerging Technology
description: Introducing AI, automation, platforms, or other **emerging technology** through disciplined experimentation, adoption design, risk management, and measurable impact.

competency.name: Innovation and Emerging Technology
competency.definition: Evaluates, pilots, and adopts new technology through evidence, risk controls, behavior change, and **measurable outcomes**.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior leaders must separate useful innovation from hype and create the operating conditions for **responsible adoption**.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you introduced a new technology that changed how work got done in your organization.
variants: Describe how you evaluated whether AI, automation, or a new platform capability was worth adopting.
Tell me about a time a technology experiment did not justify scaling.
Describe how you decided whether to build, buy, partner, or wait on an emerging capability.
Tell me about a time you introduced AI or automation outside engineering workflows.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate test **emerging technology** through hypotheses, evidence, and stage gates?
Do they integrate security, quality, adoption, and change-management concerns early?
Can they measure workflow and business impact beyond excitement or license usage?
Can they connect technology bets to strategy, opportunity cost, and portfolio choices?

scenario.signatureExample: A CTO creates a build/buy/wait portfolio for AI and automation, funding only bets with clear workflow ownership, risk controls, and measurable customer or operating impact.
context: Teams are running disconnected experiments with AI, automation, and platform tools.
Executives expect productivity and growth gains, but board pressure and vendor demos are shaping the conversation.
Security, legal, product, support, and engineering leaders disagree on what can be adopted safely.
Some ideas create business value outside engineering workflows, while others are expensive theater.
constraints: The organization needs guardrails and decision rights before broad adoption.
Impact must be measured through workflow and business outcomes, not vanity metrics.
Teams need training, workflow changes, and review behavior, not just licenses.
The leader must decide what to scale, narrow, stop, or defer based on evidence.
Portfolio choices must account for strategic differentiation, data readiness, risk, and opportunity cost.

storyAnatomy.situation: The organization had fragmented AI, automation, and platform experiments with real enthusiasm but unclear ownership, risk posture, and business impact.
storyAnatomy.task: Create an adoption model that could scale valuable **emerging technology** bets, stop weak ones, and make strategic trade-offs explicit.
action: Mapped opportunities by strategic differentiation, workflow ownership, data readiness, risk, and build/buy/wait posture.
Defined acceptable-use, security, legal, quality, and human-approval policies for each pilot class.
Ran pilots with comparison groups and measured customer impact, cycle time, review quality, operational load, defects, and user behavior.
Trained teams on effective use cases, prohibited uses, and review standards.
Stopped or narrowed experiments when evidence, risk, or adoption friction did not justify broader rollout.
Reallocated funding from disconnected demos to a small set of bets with durable leverage.
result: The organization adopted tools and workflows only where measured impact and risk posture justified it.
Security, quality, privacy, and customer-trust concerns were handled through guardrails and stop conditions.
Some attractive ideas were deferred or killed because they lacked data readiness, workflow ownership, or unit-economics evidence.
Teams gained a shared view of where AI and automation helped, where human review remained critical, and where the company should wait.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The lesson was that innovation adoption succeeds when it changes the operating model, not when it only buys a tool.
systemChange: Pilot scorecard with scale, narrow, stop, and defer thresholds.

exampleStories.title: AI-Assisted Development Adoption
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you introduced a new technology that changed how work got done in your organization.
exampleStories.situation: Engineers were already experimenting with AI coding tools, executives wanted productivity gains, and Security was concerned about code and data exposure.
strongAnswerSketch: Resist immediate company-wide rollout and define the adoption hypothesis, acceptable-use policy, and stop conditions.
Run a pilot with comparison teams, measuring review lead time, rework, defect escape, security findings, and developer experience.
Train teams on effective use cases, prohibited uses, prompt hygiene, and code-review expectations.
Scale only to workflows where evidence shows impact and reviewers can inspect the AI-assisted work.
Keep restricted repositories and sensitive customer data out of scope until enterprise controls and review behavior are proven.
whyItWorks: Manages quality and security risks during adoption.
Names conditions that would stop or narrow rollout.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I bought AI coding licenses, encouraged teams to experiment, and tracked adoption to see whether people found the tool valuable.

exampleStories.title: Customer Support Automation Pilot
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you introduced AI or automation outside engineering workflows.
exampleStories.situation: Support leaders wanted an AI summarization and routing tool to reduce backlog before renewal season, but early tests mishandled refunds, enterprise-severity cases, and PII in customer transcripts.
strongAnswerSketch: State the hypothesis: reduce p75 triage time by 20% for low-severity tickets without increasing reopens, QA overrides, privacy exceptions, or escalations.
Partner with Support, Security, Legal, and frontline agents to define eligible queues, redaction, human approval, and escalation rules before the pilot.
Run an A/B pilot against control queues and measure handle time, reopen rate, QA defects, agent trust, customer CSAT, and cost per resolved ticket.
Stop refund and enterprise-severity use cases when override rates cross the threshold, even though the original business case assumed those savings.
Scale only summarization and routing for eligible queues, then update training and add weekly exception review.
whyItWorks: Shows business empathy without accepting unsafe automation.
Uses customer and operating metrics, not only tool usage.
Includes a real residual cost: the scaled scope was smaller than the original savings case.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I gave Support access to the AI tool, asked agents to use it where helpful, and reviewed adoption and time-saved estimates after the first month.
followUpAngles: Which cases were excluded from automation?
What metric stopped part of the rollout?

exampleStories.title: Internal Platform Trial
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time a technology experiment did not justify broader rollout.
exampleStories.situation: A platform team piloted a new deployment abstraction that improved one team experience but made debugging harder for services with unusual runtime and rollback needs.
strongAnswerSketch: Define success criteria before the pilot: lead time, failure recovery, support load, and developer satisfaction.

Measure both happy-path adoption and operational friction: one pilot team cut deployment lead time by 18%, while services with unusual runtime needs doubled platform support tickets and missed the recovery-time threshold in rollback drills.
Decide not to roll out broadly until debugging, rollback, and escape-hatch problems are solved, leaving affected teams on the old path.
Document adoption criteria and rollback-drill requirements for the next platform experiment.
whyItWorks: Shows willingness to stop an exciting technology.
Uses numeric counter-evidence when the happy-path metric looked positive.
Measures operational consequences, not only developer enthusiasm.
exampleStories.weakVersion: The pilot feedback was mixed, so we delayed rollout and gave the platform team more time to improve it.
followUpAngles: Who was disappointed by the decision?
What did the next pilot do differently?

exampleStories.title: Company-Level AI Portfolio Posture
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe how you decided whether to build, buy, partner, or wait on an emerging capability.
exampleStories.situation: After a board discussion, every business unit proposed AI or automation bets, vendors pushed platform contracts, and the company had no shared view of where emerging technology created strategic leverage versus expensive theater.
strongAnswerSketch: Frame the decision as portfolio posture: build where proprietary workflow data creates advantage, buy commodity productivity tools with enterprise controls, partner where ecosystem reach matters, and wait on autonomous customer-impacting actions until evaluation and liability controls exist.
Cancel or park three executive-sponsored demos that lacked customer workflow ownership, data readiness, or unit-economics evidence.
Fund two bets with named business owners: a customer-operations copilot and an internal engineering-assistant rollout, each with stage gates, risk owners, and kill criteria.
Create investment gates for customer value, data quality, security and legal review, model evaluation, adoption behavior, unit economics, and operational support load.
Report portfolio learning quarterly: one bet scaled, one narrowed, vendor spend fell 22%, and the company had a repeatable build/buy/wait review.
whyItWorks: Illustrates the CTO level promised by the rubric.
Treats innovation as strategy and opportunity cost, not scattered pilots.
Shows principled stopping and narrowing despite executive sponsorship.
Leaves behind a durable portfolio mechanism.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I asked each business unit to propose AI use cases, selected the most promising demos, and created an innovation roadmap so executives could see momentum.
followUpAngles: Which bets did you stop or defer?
What made a bet strategic enough to build?
How did the board conversation change?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows **experimentation discipline**, adoption strategy, portfolio judgment, risk management, and measurable impact.
moves: Connects the technology bet to strategy, workflow ownership, and opportunity cost.
Explains build, buy, partner, wait, scale, narrow, or stop decisions.
Includes risk, security, quality, and human-review controls.
Measures customer, operating, and behavior outcomes, not only adoption.
Invests in training, workflow integration, and manager reinforcement.
Scales, changes, or stops based on evidence.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate treats innovation as buying tools or following trends without disciplined evaluation or adoption design.
redFlags: Uses hype language without a testable hypothesis.
Cannot explain strategic fit, opportunity cost, or build/buy/wait reasoning.
Cannot name who owned the workflow after rollout.
Cannot name conditions under which they would stop rollout.

strong: For support automation, I was testing whether low-severity summarization could cut p75 triage time by 20% without increasing reopens, QA overrides, privacy exceptions, or escalations.
For AI-assisted development, the hypothesis was not that developers would use it; it was that selected workflows would reduce review lead time while keeping defect escape and security findings flat.
weak: We wanted to see whether AI would make people more productive.
The hypothesis was that the new platform would be easier for teams and therefore worth adopting.

followUps.question: What risks did you control before adoption or scaling?

strong: We blocked sensitive repositories and customer data, required enterprise SSO and vendor terms, added code-review rules, and named stop conditions for security findings or review-quality regression.
For support automation, we limited the pilot to low-severity queues, redacted PII, kept human approval, and excluded refunds and enterprise incidents after override rates were too high.
weak: Security reviewed the tool, and we told people not to paste sensitive data into it.
We had humans check the output, so the automation risk felt manageable.

followUps.question: How did you measure impact beyond usage or enthusiasm?

strong: I compared pilot and control cohorts on review lead time, rework, defect escape, security exceptions, developer sentiment, and manager-observed workflow change.
For support, usage was secondary; we measured triage time, reopen rate, QA defects, customer CSAT, escalation load, and cost per resolved ticket.
weak: The main evidence was that most people activated the tool and reported that it saved time.
We looked at license usage, survey feedback, and a few anecdotes from teams that liked it.

followUps.question: What changed in the day-to-day workflow?

strong: We changed pull-request templates, reviewer checklists, onboarding, and manager coaching so AI-assisted output had to be inspectable rather than copied into production.
Support agents got queue-specific playbooks, override buttons, weekly exception reviews, and a clear rule for when the automation must not be used.
weak: Teams started using the tool regularly, and people said it made the work feel faster.
We published guidance and held a training session so everyone knew the recommended practices.

followUps.question: How did you decide where to build, buy, partner, or wait?

strong: We built only where proprietary workflow data or customer integration gave us durable advantage, bought commodity productivity tooling under enterprise controls, partnered for ecosystem reach, and waited on autonomous customer actions until evaluation and liability controls existed.
I made opportunity cost visible: three executive-sponsored demos lost funding because they lacked a workflow owner, data readiness, or a credible unit-economics path.
weak: We prioritized the ideas that looked most promising and matched the vendor capabilities we could buy quickly.
I let each business unit pick its best use case and then compared them in an innovation roadmap.

signals.name: Experimentation Discipline
signals.strong: Defines hypotheses, metrics, risks, comparison points, and rollout criteria.
signals.weak: Runs broad adoption based on enthusiasm or executive pressure.

signals.name: Risk-Aware Adoption
signals.strong: Integrates security, quality, privacy, and responsible-use guardrails before scaling.
signals.weak: Treats risk as a later compliance concern.

signals.name: Measurable Impact
signals.strong: Measures customer, operating, and **behavior change** outcomes.

signals.name: Strategic Portfolio Judgment
signals.strong: Connects emerging-technology bets to strategy, opportunity cost, and build/buy/wait choices.
signals.weak: Chases scattered demos without clear strategic fit, ownership, or resource trade-offs.

rubric.expected: Pilots technology within a team or adjacent workflow with clear metrics, guardrails, human-review rules, and stop conditions.
Scales or stops adoption across teams through training, workflow changes, stakeholder alignment, impact measurement, and support-load feedback.
Creates an organizational adoption model for **emerging technology** with risk controls, stage gates, and portfolio impact.
Sets company-level technology portfolio strategy, including build/buy/wait posture, strategic leverage, risk appetite, operating change, and opportunity cost.

prompts.label: What new technology or capability was being considered?
What adoption or evaluation decision did you own?
How did you test, control risk, train, and measure?
What evidence justified scaling, changing, or stopping?
What did you learn about technology adoption?
What adoption framework or guardrail remained?

relatedScenarios: Piloting support, sales, finance, or operations automation with human approval and stop criteria.
Stopping a technology rollout after pilot evidence disappoints.
Choosing a company-level build/buy/wait posture for AI or automation.
